newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl coalition partner defends Waigel's gold plan.
newsitem.headline: Kohl coalition partner defends Waigel's gold plan.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's junior coalition partners, the Free Democrats (FDP) on Friday defended Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plan to reevaulate gold reserves to help Germany qualify for European monetary union (EMU) in 1999.

FDP parliamentary leader Hermann Otto Solms told German SWF radio he was convinced the reevaulation was necessary, that it was a move nearly all European central banks had already taken, and that, for Germany, the only decision left was the timing.

Solms said such a move would create between 30 billion marks and 50 billion marks and stood by Waigel, who on Thursday said the funds would retire east German debt rather than plug budget gaps that cast doubt on Germany's ability to qualify for EMU.

His remarks came two days after the German Bundesbank issued a strongly-worded rejection of Bonn government plans to raise extra cash by revaluing the central bank assets and Bonn said it would proceed with its plan regardless.

"We must look at the facts. Do we want to abandon gains that can be achieved by a reevaulation...or do we want it -- and this should have happened earlier -- to pay off debt arising from German unification," Solms said.

He denied that the pro-business FDP, Germany's self-styled party of tax-cutting, had been partly responsible for Waigel's grab for gold because it had put pressure on the government not to raise taxes to plug budget holes.

"The row is actually only about whether this (reevaluation) should take place this year, next year or in 1999. But the point is that if these measures are right in 1999, they can not be entirely wrong in 1998," he said.

Solms said it was unfortunate that the issue of reevaulating Bundesbank assets coincided as Bonn's budgetary problems cast doubt over whether Germany would fulfil the economic criteria to help launch Europe's single currency.
